summary.one_line: A reading walkthrough of code-review-skill — how a git diff becomes an interactive HTML review document.
summary.description: This walkthrough takes a reader through the code-review-skill from input to output. The skill takes a git diff, an LLM analyzes it against a JSON contract, and a tiny Python script injects that JSON into a single HTML file with a 3-pane layout, line-attached annotations, and per-step collapsible context panels. The four full-depth storylines cover the architecture you'd want to grasp before extending the skill: the UI layout & view-mode state machine, the JSON contract that mediates LLM ↔ template, the analysis prompt that fills the contract, and the v0.3 walkthrough-annotation system that places explanations inline with code. Three smaller storylines (render pipeline, function-purpose blocks, right-pane sections) are kept at summary depth — important to know about, not central to extending the skill.

discovered_scope.note: JSON contract — defines what the LLM must produce and what the template consumes
Analysis prompt — instructs the LLM how to fill the contract
CLI entry — placeholder substitution from JSON to HTML
HTML/CSS/JS template — renders the JSON into the user-facing UI

excluded.reason: user-facing skill description; not part of the runtime pipeline
user-facing intro; redundant with SKILL.md for understanding the code
example data; useful for spot-checking but not part of the pipeline

scope.importance_criteria: Top 4 of 7 storylines selected by combined score (range 5–9). Tiebreaks favored entry_point: the template & view-mode architecture wins #1 over the JSON contract, and the analysis prompt wins #3 over the walkthrough-annotation system, because reading order benefits from grasping interaction surfaces before drilling into specific features. Summary-depth storylines (render pipeline, function-purpose blocks, right-pane sections) are still useful to know about — render.py because it's the entry point, function_purpose / right-pane sections because they're the surface a contributor would touch when adding new fields.

storylines.title: Three-pane layout and the view-mode state machine

importance_scores.rationale: centrality=3: the entire UI hangs off this layout and state model. entry_point=2: this is what the reader sees first when they open the HTML.

storylines.summary: A 280|fluid|400 grid hosts three panes; a tiny `state` object switches the center pane between PR-overview, storyline-overview, and step views.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: Think of it as a code editor split-pane: storyline tree on the left, code in the middle, sidekick context on the right. The center pane has three modes (PR overview / storyline overview / step), and a single `state.view` string decides which one renders.

purpose.evident: The grid layout (`.layout { grid-template-columns: 280px minmax(0, 1fr) 400px }`) and the `state` object near the top of the script tag together define a classic three-pane reader UI with one mutable state record. There is no router, no framework, no virtual DOM — just `rerender()` rebuilds two innerHTML strings whenever state changes.

architectural_context.system_role: User-facing UI shell. Everything else (code rendering, analysis sections, navigation) plugs into this skeleton.

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: declares the three <aside>/<main>/<aside> panes and the <script> block
fixes the 3-column grid; both side panes have independent overflow
carries the current view + selected storyline/step + collapsed-section map

architectural_context.data_flow: User clicks → navigation function (`goToPROverview`/`goToStorylineOverview`/`navigateToStep`) sets `state.view` etc. → `rerender()` rebuilds center-pane and right-pane innerHTML in one pass → `highlightCurrentNav()` re-applies `.active` classes in the left pane.

diagram.content:
user click
   │
   ▼
 goTo*() / navigateTo*()    ── mutates state
   │
   ▼
 rerender()
   ├── center-pane.innerHTML = renderPROverview / renderStorylineOverview / renderStepCenter
   ├── renderRight()
   └── highlightCurrentNav()

storylines.change_overview: The UI is a deliberately tiny SPA with no framework. The body holds three panes (left aside, center main, right aside) inside a CSS grid. A `state` object — five fields, no nesting — is the single source of truth for what's shown. Three `goTo*` / `navigateTo*` functions update the state and call `rerender()`, which sets `innerHTML` on the center pane to one of three render functions and on the right pane to one of three branches inside `renderRight()`. The pattern is small enough to read in one sitting and durable enough to support all the v0.2/v0.3 feature additions without restructuring.
storylines.reading_roadmap: S1.1 shows the layout grid + body skeleton — the bones the rest of the file decorates. S1.2 shows the `state` object and `rerender()` — the loop that ties everything together. S1.3 shows the three navigation functions that mutate state and call `rerender()`. After this storyline you should be able to predict what changes when you click any nav element.

steps.title: The three-pane grid and the body skeleton

walkthrough.explanation: Three columns, fixed-fluid-fixed. The middle column uses `minmax(0, 1fr)` rather than `1fr` so a long line of code can't force the center pane to overflow horizontally — `minmax(0, ...)` lets the column shrink below content size, which is what you want when the content has its own scroll.
Each pane scrolls on its own. This is what makes the UI work — you can scroll a long step body in the center without losing the navigation tree on the left or the analysis sections on the right.

lines.content: Select a step to see analysis.

walkthrough.explanation: Two interactive zones: the sticky header (`pr-title` + `pr-subtitle`, populated by `renderHeader()`) and the navigation tree (`nav-tree`, populated by `renderNav()`). The 'PR Overview' link is hard-coded as a sibling because it's the only nav element that exists outside the per-storyline tree.

Just a `<main>` element. `rerender()` overwrites its innerHTML wholesale on every navigation. There is no DOM diffing — the file is small enough that brute-force innerHTML replacement is fine and keeps the code readable.

steps.summary: The HTML body declares three siblings inside a CSS grid: a left `<aside>` with header + nav tree, a `<main>` center pane, and a right `<aside>`. Each pane scrolls independently.
invariants: All content lives inside `.layout` — there is no element outside the grid.
Each pane has `overflow-y: auto` and `height: 100vh` so they scroll independently.
The center pane's content is always replaced wholesale by `rerender()`; it has no persistent DOM.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: This skeleton is what loads when the user opens the rendered HTML in a browser. The empty 'Loading...' placeholders sit there until `init()` fires `renderHeader()` + `renderNav()` + `goToPROverview()` (line 1430).
implicit_dependencies: `renderHeader()` assumes elements with id `pr-title` and `pr-subtitle` exist.
All `rerender*` functions write innerHTML to `#center-pane` and `#right-pane`.

design_rationale.approach: Use a small SPA framework (Vue/React/Svelte) instead of vanilla DOM
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: A framework would make the state→view binding declarative. The cost is a build step, a runtime, and a much larger output file. The skill's hard constraint is *single self-contained HTML, no servers, no build tools* (SKILL.md), so vanilla DOM is the correct choice — and the file is small enough that the absence of declarative binding doesn't hurt readability.

steps.title: The state object and the rerender loop

lines.content: // Right-pane section collapse state, keyed by section name
// Find the section element and toggle its class — avoids full re-render

function_purpose.problem_solved: Track per-section collapse state with sensible defaults, and apply toggles without forcing a full center+right re-render.
function_purpose.without_it: Either every section would render expanded (right pane becomes too long to scan) or toggling would require a full rerender (which would scroll the user back to the top of the right pane every click — annoying when reading).

walkthrough.explanation: This is the entire integration point with `render.py`. The Python script does a simple text replace on `/*REVIEW_DATA_PLACEHOLDER*/`, substituting the JSON. From this line down, the template can pretend the data was always there as a global constant. No fetch, no async, no error path — just a plain JS literal.

Five fields. No nesting beyond `sectionCollapsed`. Every navigation function mutates this object and calls `rerender()`. Everything you see on screen is a deterministic projection of these five fields.

Note what's collapsed by default: the long factual sections (`usage_context`, `test_coverage`, `codebase_patterns`, `alternative_approaches`) and `analysis`. The opinion-light sections (summary, evaluation, suggestions, behavior_delta, prerequisites, concerns) stay expanded. This is a calibration of what the reviewer most needs at a glance.

Notice this does NOT call `rerender()`. It mutates `state.sectionCollapsed` and toggles a CSS class on one DOM node. This is the one place the template breaks its 'state changes → full innerHTML replacement' rule, and it does so because forcing a full rerender on every section toggle would scroll the user away from where they were reading.

steps.summary: The `state` object has five fields. `DEFAULT_COLLAPSED` configures which right-pane sections start collapsed. `isCollapsed`/`toggleSection` provide the section-collapse API; `toggleSection` deliberately avoids `rerender()` to preserve scroll position.
invariants: `state.view` is always one of the three string literals (`'pr_overview' | 'storyline_overview' | 'step'`).
When `state.view === 'step'`, both `currentStorylineId` and `currentStepId` are non-null.
When `state.view === 'pr_overview'`, both `currentStorylineId` and `currentStepId` are null.
`sectionCollapsed[name]` overrides `DEFAULT_COLLAPSED` once the user has explicitly toggled that section.

key_data_structures.name: state
key_data_structures.shape: { view: string, currentStorylineId: string|null, currentStepId: string|null, sectionCollapsed: Map<string, bool> }
key_data_structures.role: Single source of truth for what the UI shows. Reading any render code starts with knowing what's in here.

key_data_structures.name: DEFAULT_COLLAPSED
key_data_structures.role: Configures the per-section default collapse state. To change defaults, edit only this set; renderers consult it via `isCollapsed()`.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Every navigation/interaction starts by mutating `state` and ends by calling `rerender()` (or, for section toggles, by mutating one CSS class).

callers.context: All three navigation entry points mutate `state` then call `rerender()`.
Every right-pane section header binds its onclick to `toggleSection`, which uses `isCollapsed` and the `state.sectionCollapsed` map.

call_patterns: Mutation-then-rerender: every nav function follows this exact pattern.
Section toggle is the only mutation that does NOT trigger rerender.
implicit_dependencies: All render functions read from `state` directly rather than receiving it as an argument.
Collapse state survives navigation (it lives on `state`) but does not survive page reload — there is no localStorage.

codebase_patterns.convention_alignment: The single-state-object + idempotent-rerender pattern is the same pattern Elm/early React popularized. Here it's implemented in ~5 lines of vanilla JS rather than via a framework.

design_rationale.approach: Persist `sectionCollapsed` to localStorage so collapse state survives page reload
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: A reviewer typically reads a PR once, so reload-survival is low-value. The simpler in-memory map keeps the state model trivially auditable. The reading-mode sibling skill makes the opposite call because reading walkthroughs are revisited.
Consistency (one mutation pattern) vs. UX (rerender resets scroll). The author chose UX, paying the small cost of a one-off branch in the toggle code.

prerequisites.summary: From S1.1: the center and right panes have ids `center-pane` and `right-pane`. The render functions in this step (and S1.3) write innerHTML to those ids.

steps.title: Navigation functions and rerender()

function_purpose.problem_solved: Make every state change converge on a single deterministic projection of the UI, so that any navigation action's effect is exactly: 'mutate state, then redraw center + right pane from scratch.'
function_purpose.without_it: Without a single rerender entry point, every navigation function would have to know which DOM nodes to update and in what order, multiplying bug surface. With it, you can confidently add a new view mode by adding one branch to the `if/else` chain.

walkthrough.explanation: All three nav functions are the same shape: set fields on `state`, call `rerender()`. `navigateToStep` adds two guards (null id, missing step) because it can be called from prerequisite jump-links and keyboard shortcuts where the target may not exist.

A flat if/else over `state.view`. Each branch sets `center.innerHTML`. There's no fall-through, no default — if a new view mode is added, the developer must add a branch here, which is a feature not a bug (forces explicit handling).

`_fileBlockSeq` is a module-level counter used to generate unique ids for walkthrough-annotation toggle scoping. Resetting it on every rerender prevents the counter from growing unboundedly, and ensures the same step always gets the same block ids — useful if any external code wants to deep-link.

Every navigation resets both panes to the top. This is the right default for navigating to a *new* view, but it's exactly why `toggleSection()` (S1.2) avoids calling `rerender()` — toggling a section open/closed should NOT scroll the reader away.

steps.summary: Three navigation functions mutate `state` then call `rerender()`. `rerender()` clears the file-block id counter, dispatches on `state.view` to write `center.innerHTML`, calls `renderRight()`, fixes nav highlights, and resets scroll.
invariants: Every state mutation exits through `rerender()` (except `toggleSection`).
After `rerender()` returns, the DOM is a pure function of `state` and `REVIEW_DATA`.
`_fileBlockSeq` is reset to 0 at the start of every rerender.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Called from every onclick handler in the left nav and from keyboard shortcuts (lines 1402–1420). `init()` calls `goToPROverview()` once at the end of page load.

callers.context: `init()` performs first paint by triggering a navigation.

call_patterns: Always invoked from a synchronous onclick or keydown — there are no async navigation paths.
Section-toggle is the one mutation that bypasses rerender (see S1.2).
implicit_dependencies: Every render function reads `state` and `REVIEW_DATA` directly, so they all rely on the rerender contract that those globals are coherent at call time.

prerequisites.summary: From S1.2: `state.view`, `currentStorylineId`, `currentStepId` are the fields each nav function mutates. `_fileBlockSeq` is a counter the walkthrough-annotation system (S4) uses for unique ids.

storylines.title: The JSON contract — the seam between LLM and template

importance_scores.rationale: centrality=3: every other component reads or writes this shape. conceptual_weight=3: the design of this contract is what makes the skill work — it encodes both the analyst's job and the template's render plan.

storylines.summary: A versioned JSON shape with metadata, summary, and an array of storylines, each containing storyline-level context plus an array of steps with code views, factual context, and analytical sections.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: The schema is the *contract* between two parties that never talk directly: an LLM that produces JSON, and a static HTML file that consumes it. Designing this contract is the actual product. v0.3 added line-attached annotations (`walkthrough`) and function-level rationale (`function_purpose`) — both attached to the `FileView` so that any code shown anywhere can carry them.

purpose.stated: From schema.md line 1: 'This is the JSON contract between the analysis prompt and the HTML template.'
purpose.evident: Two consumers of this shape are both visible in the codebase: `analyze_diff.md` instructs the LLM how to fill it, and `review.html` reads from it. The schema's structure mirrors the UI: top-level → metadata + summary; each storyline → its own page; each step → its own page; FileView → its own code block.

architectural_context.system_role: Cross-component contract. Sits between the analysis phase (LLM) and the rendering phase (template).

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: consumer-as-producer — instructs the LLM to generate this shape

architectural_context.data_flow: schema.md → analyst LLM produces JSON → render.py injects → review.html reads. The schema is the only doc that both parties must agree on; it's the static dependency that makes the dynamic pipeline work.

storylines.change_overview: The schema is structured in tiers that mirror the UI: top-level metadata + summary + storylines[]; each storyline carries its overview fields (purpose, architectural_context, change_overview, reading_roadmap, plus v0.2's storyline-level confidence); each step carries its code views and the right-pane sections (behavior_delta, usage_context, test_coverage, codebase_patterns, alternative_approaches, evaluation, suggestions, analysis, concerns, prerequisites). v0.3 added two FileView-level fields, `function_purpose` and `walkthrough`, attaching rationale and inline annotations to any code block — this is what gives the v0.3 output its distinctive 'reading' feel.
storylines.reading_roadmap: S2.1 shows the top-level + storyline-level shape — what wraps everything. S2.2 shows the step-level shape and FileView with its v0.3 additions — where the line-by-line work lives. After this storyline you should be able to predict exactly what JSON the analysis prompt must emit.

steps.title: Top-level shape: metadata, summary, storylines

walkthrough.explanation: Just four top-level keys. `schema_version` is a string the template can branch on if/when the contract evolves (it doesn't currently — backward compat is achieved by gracefully handling missing fields). `metadata`, `summary`, and `storylines` are the three real payload sections.

lines.content: "kind": "feature | fix | refactor | test | config | doc | mixed",
"stated":      "string | null (what PR description / commit messages claim)",
"evident":     "string (what the code structure actually shows the change does)",
"discrepancy": "string | null (if stated and evident differ; null if aligned)"
"system_role":     "string (what part of the system this change touches)",
"data_flow":       "string | null (high-level prose describing flow through this change)",
"change_overview":  "string (multiple paragraphs OK — what the storyline does as a whole)",
"reading_roadmap":  "string (each step's role and how they connect)",

walkthrough.explanation: An id (used for prerequisite jump-links), a title, a kind (drives the badge color), a confidence + reasoning (this is honest about how cohesive the grouping is — a 'low' confidence storyline is the schema's way of admitting 'these changes are bundled but not really related').

Four fields added in v0.2 to give the reviewer the *shape* of the storyline before they dive into steps. `purpose` separates *stated* from *evident* — the discrepancy field is high-value because it surfaces 'PR claims X, code does Y' mismatches. `architectural_context` lets the storyline narrate which modules are involved at what role, with an optional Mermaid diagram for graph-shaped changes.

`change_overview` is multi-paragraph; `reading_roadmap` is a one-line tour of how the steps connect. Both render on the storyline-overview page, between the architectural-context block and the step roadmap.

steps.summary: Top level has four keys: `schema_version`, `metadata`, `summary`, `storylines[]`. Each storyline has identity fields (id/title/kind/confidence/summary/files_touched), a v0.2 storyline-level context block (purpose, architectural_context, change_overview, reading_roadmap), and `steps[]`.
invariants: Every storyline has at least one step (validated in analyze_diff.md phase 9).
Storyline `id`s are unique within the document.
`purpose.discrepancy` is null when `stated` and `evident` align.

key_data_structures.name: Storyline
key_data_structures.shape: { id, title, kind, confidence, summary, files_touched[], purpose, architectural_context, change_overview, reading_roadmap, steps[] }
key_data_structures.role: The unit of grouping. Each storyline gets its own overview page in the UI.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Read by the template's `renderPROverview` (lists all storylines as cards) and `renderStorylineOverview` (renders one storyline's full overview page).

design_rationale.approach: Use a JSON Schema file (json-schema.org) instead of prose-in-markdown
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: JSON Schema gives machine-readable validation but loses the explanatory prose that makes the contract usable by an LLM. Since the producer is an LLM (not a typed program), prose-with-examples is more directly useful. The cost is no automatic schema validation.

steps.title: Step shape and the FileView with v0.3 additions

lines.content: // NEW in v0.3 — function-level rationale (optional; omit if not function-scoped)
"function_name": "string | null",   // e.g. "MemTable::Add"; null if not function-scoped
"problem_solved": "string (what problem this function exists to solve — motivation, not description)",
"without_it":     "string (what would happen / what callers would do if this didn't exist)",
// when structure == "multi_section" — function does multiple things
// NEW in v0.3 — code-attached walk-through annotations (optional)
"explanation": "string (substantial paragraph: what this chunk does AND why this way)"

walkthrough.explanation: A FileView always carries a path, a language, a line range, and an array of `{line_num, content, change}` rows. The `change` enum is what lets the same shape render both diffs (`added`/`removed`) and plain reading (`unchanged`).

Two fields, `problem_solved` and `without_it`, force articulation of motivation that descriptive comments usually skip. `multi_section` exists for long historically-merged functions where one rationale wouldn't capture the whole — each section gets its own pair, scoped to a line range.

An array of `{line_start, line_end, chunk_role, explanation}`. The schema spec text further down (lines 206–218) emphasizes these should be SPARSE and change-centric: 'does understanding this chunk help the reader understand the change?' If yes, annotate; if no, skip. This keeps annotations as signal, not noise.

lines.content: Walk-through annotations are **change-centric with related unchanged code included**.
For each candidate chunk, the agent asks: "Does understanding this chunk help the
- **Yes** (chunk is a +/- change, OR unchanged code the change interacts with) → annotate
- **No** (surrounding context unrelated to the change's logic) → skip
This makes walk-through **sparse**, not exhaustive. A 30-line function with a 5-line
change might have 2-3 annotations. Avoid both failure modes:
- "Annotate only +/- lines" → reader still can't connect change to surrounding logic
- `problem_solved` is **motivation** ("the system needs Y; this function provides Y").
`without_it` is **counter-factual** ("if this didn't exist, callers would pay cost /
risk error / be unable to do thing"). Together they force articulation of non-obvious value.
- For `multi_section`, sections reflect the agent's reading of the function's logical
structure (not necessarily aligned with diff hunks). E.g. a 200-line function with
parsing in lines 1-80 and execution in 81-200 gets two sections.
- Use `single` when the function has one coherent purpose. Use `multi_section` for

supporting_definitions.why_included: The scope heuristic is the part of the spec that most directly governs annotation quality. Without it, agents tend toward exhaustive line-by-line annotation, which destroys the value.

steps.summary: FileView carries the actual code: file path, language, line range, and a `lines[]` array. v0.3 added `function_purpose` (problem_solved + without_it, optionally multi-section) and `walkthrough[]` (sparse line-attached annotations).
invariants: `walkthrough[i].line_start <= walkthrough[i].line_end <= context_end_line`.
`function_purpose.structure === 'multi_section'` implies `sections[]` is non-empty and covers logical regions of the file.
Annotations are sparse — the spec explicitly forbids line-by-line narration.

key_data_structures.name: FileView
key_data_structures.shape: { file, language, context_start_line, context_end_line, lines[], function_purpose?, walkthrough[]? }
key_data_structures.role: The smallest renderable unit of code. Every code block in the UI corresponds to one FileView.

key_data_structures.name: WalkthroughAnnotation
key_data_structures.role: Inline annotation tied to a line range. Renders as a row inside the code table after `line_end`.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Read by `renderFileBlock` (review.html line 1056) which renders one FileView as a `.file-block` card with header, optional function-purpose block, optional walkthrough-controls bar, and the code table.

callers.context: Each step iterates its primary_changes array, rendering one FileView per entry.
Supporting definitions follow the same shape as primary_changes (FileViewWithReason adds `why_included`) and render with `isReference=true` for visually distinct styling.

call_patterns: FileView is always rendered inside a step's center pane.
When `function_purpose` is omitted, the function-purpose block simply doesn't render — the template handles missing fields by not emitting markup.
implicit_dependencies: Walkthrough annotations are anchored on `line_end` (renderFileBlock builds an index by `line_end` to know where to insert the annotation row).

codebase_patterns.convention_alignment: Optional fields in this schema render as nothing-on-screen when absent — there's no 'no annotations' placeholder. The renderer checks truthiness on every optional and emits empty string if missing.

design_rationale.approach: Put `walkthrough` annotations at the step level rather than the FileView level
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: If a step had multiple files, step-level annotations would need to carry a file path. FileView-level annotations don't — they're scoped to the FileView's own lines. The cost is duplication if the same annotation logically applies to multiple FileViews; in practice annotations are file-specific so this isn't a real cost.

prerequisites.summary: From S2.1: storylines contain steps[]; each step contains code_view, which carries the FileView arrays this step describes.

storylines.title: The analysis prompt — how the LLM fills the contract

importance_scores.rationale: entry_point=2 wins the tiebreak vs S4 (walkthrough rendering): the prompt is closer to the user-facing entry of the analysis pipeline than the v0.3 rendering feature.

storylines.summary: A 9-phase prompt walks the LLM from reading the diff to emitting JSON, with explicit dual roles (research assistant + senior reviewer) and length expectations per field.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: Think of analyze_diff.md as a recipe card the LLM reads once before cooking. It tells the LLM what to read first (the whole diff), what shape to produce (schema-conformant JSON), what voice to use in each field (factual vs opinion), and which failure modes to avoid (generic suggestions, padded analysis, fabricated alternatives).

purpose.evident: The prompt is structured as 9 phases. Phases 1–3 establish input + grouping. Phases 4–7 build content per step (factual, then analytical). Phases 8–9 finalize. Length expectations and a 'common failure modes' list at the bottom calibrate the LLM's output verbosity.

architectural_context.system_role: The 'how to do the job' instructions for the analysis phase. Sits between the user's trigger ('review this PR') and the JSON output.

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: calibration — how long each field should be
guard rails against obvious LLM failure modes

architectural_context.data_flow: User trigger → SKILL.md selects this prompt → LLM reads diff + repo + this prompt + schema.md → emits JSON.

storylines.change_overview: This file is essentially a workflow + style guide for the LLM. The headline design choice is the *dual role* declaration up top: 'You are simultaneously: 1. A research assistant ... 2. A senior reviewer.' This tells the LLM to keep factual fields (behavior_delta, callers, test coverage) honest and concrete, and analytical fields (evaluation, suggestions, concerns) pointed and evidence-grounded. The 9 phases enforce a sensible order (read everything before grouping; group before scoring; score before deepening per step). The bottom of the file calibrates verbosity per field — explicit numbers like '1–5 callers typical' prevent both too-sparse and too-bloated outputs.
storylines.reading_roadmap: S3.1 shows the dual-role declaration and phase 1 — what voice the LLM is asked to use, and what input to read. S3.2 shows phases 6–7 where factual research and analytical opinion are kept structurally separate, plus the calibration block that prevents typical LLM length-failure modes.

steps.title: The dual role declaration and the read-first phase

lines.content: You are analyzing a code diff to produce a rich, structured review document.
Your goal is to give a reviewer **enough context to confidently judge a
change, even if they're not deeply familiar with the codebase**.
1. A **research assistant** — locating callers, tests, similar patterns,
establishing the change's place in the system. This is mostly
2. A **senior reviewer** — forming opinions about quality, raising concerns,
suggesting improvements, identifying landmines. This is *analytical* work.
Both roles matter. Don't shortchange either.
- Repo path (read surrounding code as needed)
A single JSON document conforming to schema v0.2. Includes per-storyline
Read the entire diff. Don't start grouping until you've seen all changes.
For each changed file, also read the **full file** from the post-change
working tree. You'll need this to find enclosing functions, identify
referenced symbols, and produce code views with proper context.

walkthrough.explanation: This is the design move that distinguishes this prompt from a generic 'review code' instruction. By naming two roles explicitly and noting the work-type for each (factual vs analytical), the prompt prevents the LLM from collapsing both into a vague middle voice. Each schema field in S2 maps cleanly to one role or the other; the prompt later instructs the LLM to keep them separate in tone.

'Don't start grouping until you've seen all changes' is doing real work: it prevents the LLM from prematurely committing to a grouping based on the first few hunks it reads. Reading the *full file* (not just the diff) is what enables the rest of the schema — you can't fill `function_purpose` or pick supporting_definitions without seeing the surrounding code.

steps.summary: The opening of the prompt declares two roles (research assistant + senior reviewer), lists the inputs (diff + repo + schema), and starts the workflow with a strict read-everything-first phase.
invariants: The LLM reads the *entire* diff before grouping (phase 1 explicit).
For each changed file, the LLM also reads the post-change full file (needed for enclosing-function context).

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Loaded by the SKILL.md workflow when the user triggers a review.
implicit_dependencies: This prompt assumes schema.md is also loaded as context.

design_rationale.approach: Single-role prompt ('You are a senior code reviewer')
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: A single role would simplify the prompt but blur the line between factual and analytical fields, which is exactly the line the v0.2 schema invests in. The dual frame buys structural honesty in the output.

steps.title: Phase 6/7 separation and the calibration block

lines.content: ### Phase 6: Build factual context for each step
This is the **research assistant** work. For each step:
- `before`: how did this code behave before the change? Plain language.
- `diff`: the meaningful functional delta — not the text diff. Example:
"Before: `Get()` would return KeyNotFound if the seq was newer than
any tracked. After: it returns the most-recent record regardless of
seq, falling back to KeyNotFound only if no record exists."
### Phase 7: Build analytical content for each step
This is the **senior reviewer** work. The fields here can be substantive
when the step warrants it. Don't pad — but don't shortchange a complex

walkthrough.explanation: Phase 6 says 'this is the research assistant work'. Phase 7 says 'this is the senior reviewer work'. The two phases populate different schema fields. By structuring the prompt this way, the LLM has to mentally switch voice between phases rather than smearing both voices across every field.

lines.content: For a complex step in a non-trivial codebase:
- `behavior_delta`: a sentence or two per field
- `analysis`: a paragraph or two when substantive
For trivial steps (rename, comment fix), most fields can be brief or null.

walkthrough.explanation: Explicit numeric ranges per field. This is what prevents LLM outputs from being either skeletal (all 1-sentence fields) or bloated (every field a 5-paragraph essay). LLMs tend toward unhelpful symmetry — saying the same amount about every field regardless of substance — and explicit ranges break that tendency.

Equally important: 'For trivial steps ... brief or null'. Explicitly licensing the LLM to skip fields prevents the LLM from manufacturing fake content for trivial changes (a known failure mode for verbose LLMs).

steps.summary: Phases 6 and 7 split factual research from analytical opinion structurally. The 'Length expectations' block at the bottom calibrates each field with explicit ranges and an escape valve for trivial steps.
invariants: Phase 6 fields are factual; phase 7 fields are analytical. The prompt does not blur these.
`behavior_delta` is the only field marked 'always populate' — the prompt allows nulling everything else when the step doesn't warrant it.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Read by the LLM during analysis. The length expectations especially shape verbosity calibration.

steps.analysis: The phase 6/7 split is doing more work than it looks like. By naming the role of each phase ('research assistant', 'senior reviewer') and the work-type ('evidenced/factual', 'analytical'), the prompt aligns the LLM's voice with the schema's structural separation. This is harder to achieve with a flat 'fill in these fields' prompt — LLMs tend to apply the same voice everywhere unless instructed otherwise. The explicit phase headers also let the agent self-check: 'I'm in phase 7, so this should be opinion not fact.'

prerequisites.summary: From S3.1: the prompt declared two roles up front. The phase 6/7 split is where those roles are operationalized into actual schema fields.

storylines.title: The walkthrough-annotation rendering system

importance_scores.rationale: novelty=3: line-attached annotations rendered inside a code table is the v0.3 differentiator — this is the part that visually separates the skill from GitHub's PR view.

storylines.summary: `renderFileBlock` builds a code `<table>`, indexes annotations by `line_end`, and inserts each annotation as a `<tr colspan=3>` row right after the matching code line.
storylines.mental_model_anchor: Imagine you're reading a code listing in a textbook with margin notes. The table shows code rows, but every now and then a 'note' row interrupts to explain what just happened. Here those notes are styled rows with colspan=3 spanning the full code-table width, and they live inside the same `<table>` so they scroll naturally with the code.

purpose.evident: The function `renderFileBlock` (review.html lines 1056–1131) produces one `.file-block` card. Inside it a `<table class="code-table">` holds normal code rows; walkthrough annotations are rendered as additional rows interleaved with the code rows. The implementation handles three subtle cases: (1) a modified line (added+removed) shows as two rows with the same `line_num`, so annotations must anchor on the LAST matching row; (2) annotations are individually collapsible; (3) a controls bar offers 'Hide all'/'Show all' scoped to one file-block.

architectural_context.system_role: Per-file rendering layer. Used by both primary_changes and supporting_definitions in every step view.

involved_modules.role_in_storyline: main entry point — builds the file-block card
renders the v0.3 function_purpose block above the code table

architectural_context.data_flow: step.code_view → for each FileView → renderFileBlock(fv, isReference) → emit `.file-block` card with file-header + (optional) function_purpose + (optional) wt-controls + code-table containing interleaved code rows and annotation rows.

storylines.change_overview: The interesting part of `renderFileBlock` is how walkthrough annotations are placed. Annotations carry a `line_end` field. The code builds a map `annByRowIndex` that maps a TABLE ROW INDEX (not a line number) to the annotation that should appear after that row. The mapping is established by iterating `fv.lines[]` forward and recording the LAST row whose `line_num === ann.line_end`. This last-match rule handles the case where a modified line shows up twice (once as a 'removed' row and once as an 'added' row, sharing the same line_num) — without it the annotation would render after the 'removed' row, leaving the 'added' row dangling.
storylines.reading_roadmap: S4.1 walks `renderFileBlock`'s row-build loop, focusing on the annotation-insertion logic. S4.2 shows the toggle handlers — how clicking on an annotation row collapses just that annotation, and the per-block 'Hide all' button.

steps.title: renderFileBlock — annotation indexing and row interleaving

lines.content: // v0.3: Walkthrough annotations. A modified line shows up as two rows
// (one "removed" and one "added") that share the same line_num. To avoid
// emitting the same annotation twice, map each annotation to the LAST
// row index whose line_num matches ann.line_end, and only insert there.
// v0.3: walkthrough controls bar (only if annotations exist)
// Build code rows, interleaving walkthrough annotations after the corresponding line_end

function_purpose.problem_solved: Place each walkthrough annotation as a separate row inside the same `<table>` as the code, immediately after the line it annotates.
function_purpose.without_it: If annotations were rendered outside the table, they wouldn't track scroll with the code or share width with the code lines. If they were rendered inline within a code line, the explanation would compete with the code for horizontal space.

walkthrough.explanation: Build `annByRowIndex` — a map from ROW INDEX (not line number) to annotation. The forward iteration with last-write-wins is the key trick: when a line is modified, fv.lines[] contains both the old (`removed`) and new (`added`) row sharing `line_num`, and we want the annotation to anchor to the *new* (later) row, not the *old* one.
Standard code row: line number, change marker (+/−/space), content. The class `line-${line.change}` colors the row green/red/transparent.

Right after pushing the code row, check if this row index has an annotation in the map. If so, push a `<tr><td colspan=3>` row containing the annotation card. The annotation lives inside the `<table>` so it shares horizontal width with code rows and respects natural document flow.

supporting_definitions.why_included: Shows the function's setup — `blockId` is the unique scoping id used by `toggleAllAnnotations` to scope its DOM query. `_fileBlockSeq` is the module-level counter reset by every rerender (S1.3).

steps.summary: Two passes over `fv.lines[]`: the first builds `annByRowIndex` mapping each annotation to its target row index (last-match wins); the second emits code rows and inserts annotation rows after the matching code row.
invariants: An annotation's target row index is the LAST row whose `line_num === ann.line_end` (handles modified-line double rows).
Annotation rows live inside the same `<table>` as code rows, with `colspan=3` to span the full code-table width.
If `fv.walkthrough` is missing or empty, no annotation rows are emitted and no controls bar renders.

key_data_structures.name: annByRowIndex
key_data_structures.role: Maps a row index in the emitted table to the annotation that should follow it. Built once per FileView, indexed by table-row position not line number.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Called from `renderStepCenter` (line 991) for each entry in `step.code_view.primary_changes` and `step.code_view.supporting_definitions`.

callers.context: primary changes — main code blocks for the step
supporting definitions — referenced code shown for context

call_patterns: Called once per FileView. A step typically has 1–3 primary_changes and 0–3 supporting_definitions.
`isReference` flag toggles the dashed border + 'reference' label — purely visual.
implicit_dependencies: Reads `_fileBlockSeq` (module-level counter, reset by `rerender()`) for blockId generation.
`toggleAllAnnotations` uses `blockId` to scope its querySelectorAll — annotation toggles in different file-blocks don't interfere.

design_rationale.approach: Render annotations as siblings of the table rather than rows inside it
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: Sibling-of-table would lose horizontal alignment with code and break natural scroll flow. Inside-the-table requires the colspan=3 trick but keeps everything visually anchored. The chosen design is harder to write and easier to read.

design_rationale.approach: Index annotations by line_num instead of by row index
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: By line_num would re-introduce the modified-line double-row bug (annotation would attach to the first matching row, leaving the second one dangling). Indexing by *last* matching row index is the deliberate fix; the comment block at lines 1066–1069 explicitly documents this.

steps.analysis: The forward-iterate-and-track-last pattern is doing surprisingly subtle work. A naive implementation (index by line_num once) would silently mis-anchor annotations on every modified line. The bug would be invisible for added-only or removed-only lines, surface only when the same line_num appeared twice, and even then might look 'fine' to a casual eye — the annotation just appears after the wrong row. The author preempted this by writing the comment first (lines 1066–1069) and the fix second.

prerequisites.summary: From S2.2: each `walkthrough[]` entry has `line_start`, `line_end`, `chunk_role`, `explanation`. The renderer anchors annotations on `line_end`.
From S1.3: `_fileBlockSeq` is reset at the start of every `rerender()`, so blockIds are stable per render but reset between navigations.

steps.title: Per-annotation and per-block toggle handlers

lines.content: // v0.3: Show/hide all annotations in a file-block

walkthrough.explanation: Climbs from the clicked toggle span to the enclosing `.wt-annotation` div, toggles the `wt-collapsed` class (which the CSS uses to hide `.wt-explanation`), and updates the toggle character. Uses no central state — the source of truth is the DOM class itself.

Scoped by `blockId`: the function only touches annotations inside that one file-block. Two file-blocks on the same step have independent 'Hide all' / 'Show all' state — clicking 'Hide all' on one doesn't affect the other. This is why `_fileBlockSeq` (S1.3) needs to generate unique ids per render.

steps.summary: Two toggle handlers: one collapses one annotation (climbs DOM from the clicked toggle span), the other scoping by blockId to collapse/expand every annotation within one file-block. Neither uses the JS `state` object — the DOM class is the source of truth.
invariants: Annotation collapse state is per-DOM-node, not stored in JS state.
Block-scoped toggles only affect annotations inside the matching `blockId`.
Toggle character (`▸` vs `▾`) and the `wt-collapsed` class stay in sync.

usage_context.primary_usage_scenario: Called from inline onclick handlers inside the rendered annotation rows and the per-block 'Hide all' / 'Show all' buttons.
call_patterns: Always invoked from a synchronous click handler.
State lives in DOM classes, not in the JS `state` object.
implicit_dependencies: Annotation collapse state does NOT survive `rerender()` — every navigation rebuilds the DOM and re-emits annotations as expanded.
This is intentional: navigating to a new step is a fresh reading context, so resetting annotation visibility makes sense.

codebase_patterns.convention_alignment: Section-collapse state (in `state.sectionCollapsed`) survives navigation but annotation collapse state does not. The asymmetry reflects intent: section preferences are user choices about the right-pane layout; annotation visibility is per-step reading context.

design_rationale.approach: Store annotation collapse state in `state.sectionCollapsed`-style map
design_rationale.tradeoff_vs_chosen_design: DOM-as-state is simpler when state is per-DOM-node and doesn't need to survive rerenders. The rerender contract (S1.3) explicitly resets annotation visibility, which is the desired behavior — saving collapse state across navigations would mean the user re-opens a step and finds annotations they hid 10 minutes ago, which is more confusing than helpful.

prerequisites.summary: From S4.1: each annotation row has class `.wt-annotation` and `data-block-id`. The toggle handlers use these as DOM selectors.

storylines.title: The render pipeline — JSON to HTML in 60 lines

importance_scores.rationale: entry_point=3: this is the actual CLI binary. Kept at summary depth because the implementation itself is a 60-line placeholder substitution — easy to read in full from render.py without a walkthrough.

storylines.summary: `render.py` is a single-file CLI that takes (input.json, output.html) on argv. It loads the JSON, loads `template/review.html`, finds `/*REVIEW_DATA_PLACEHOLDER*/` once, json-dumps the data with `ensure_ascii=False` and a `</` → `<\/` escape (to prevent JSON content from prematurely closing the embedding `<script>` tag), substitutes only the first occurrence, and writes the output. Errors at any step exit with code 1. The script intentionally does not validate the JSON shape — it trusts the analysis prompt's output and lets template rendering fail loudly if the contract is broken.

storylines.title: Function-purpose blocks (renderFunctionPurpose)
storylines.summary: `renderFunctionPurpose(fp)` (review.html lines 1020–1054) renders the v0.3 `function_purpose` block above the code table. Two structures: `single` emits a flat `problem_solved` + `without_it` pair; `multi_section` emits a sub-block per section, each with its own line range and pair. The block has its own background color (`#f0f6ff`), a small tag (`function purpose` / `multi-section`), and the function name in monospace. It renders nothing if `fp` is null — so a FileView without function_purpose just shows code straight after the file header. To extend the function_purpose semantics (e.g. add a `complexity` field), this is the place to render it.

storylines.title: Right-pane analysis sections (renderRight)

importance_scores.rationale: total=5: kept at summary because the section-rendering code is repetitive and easily understood by reading any one section as a template for the rest.

storylines.summary: `renderRight()` (review.html lines 1176–1352) is a long but flat dispatch. For each schema field that has content (`prerequisites`, `summary`, `behavior_delta`, `usage_context`, `test_coverage`, `codebase_patterns`, `alternative_approaches`, `evaluation`, `suggestions`, `analysis`, `concerns`), it builds an HTML string and pushes it onto a `sections[]` array using the `section()` helper (which wraps content in a collapsible `.analysis-section` block). The function reads `state.view` to pick between three branches: pr_overview shows a placeholder, storyline_overview shows a 'Storyline at a glance' summary, and step view emits all the analysis sections. To add a new schema field that should render in the right pane, you add a new block in the step branch and a CSS class for the new section type.
